text: (a) Τὴν εἰς ἄλλους γιγνομένην θεοσημείαν. Sic quoque Turrian. Miraculum a Salvatore Deo factum aliis. Mihi tamen non suadeo, quin legam, εἰς ἀνθρώπους. Nam quæ exempla ponit Maximus, τὴν ἀνάστασιν, τὴν ἀνάληψιν: resurrectionem in cœlum receptionem, secundum ejus verum et planum sensum, ipsa vere divina signa et miracula, non εἰς ἄλλους exhibita dici possint in alios; bene tamen εἰς ἀνθρώπους, in homines: nam et ipse vere homo Salvator Deus, sic virtute divinitatis sanci-tatus, ut Paulus testis est, et in cœlum levatus. Decoquit Turrianus. Qui de aliorum suscitatione et curatione exponeret (nam et ἀνάληψις probatis auctoribus et grammaticis θεραπεία est, et ἀνάρρωσις) nihil quidem is peccaret retinendo εἰς ἄλλους, quod et mihi primum placuerat: sed id durius-culum, et remotius a Maximi ecclesiastica styli simplicitate, qua libenter sacris ipsis ac receptis vocibus utatur: alias proclive admodum mutari τὸ ἀνοῦς breviatum, quod est, ἀνθρώπους, in ἄλλους
anchorLine: τὴν εἰς ἄλλους [ἀνθρώπους] τῷ Σωτῆρι Θεῷ γινομένην θεοσημείαν (a) · οἷον, τὴν ἀνάστασιν, ἢ τὴν ἀνάληψιν
en: On ‘the sign [of God] done toward others’ (Τὴν εἰς ἄλλους γιγνομένην θεοσημείαν). So too Turrianus: ‘a miracle done by the Saviour God in [or: for] others.’ I cannot, however, persuade myself not to read εἰς ἀνθρώπους. For the examples Maximus gives, ‘the resurrection, the ascension’ (that is, the resurrection and the reception into heaven), according to their true and plain sense, are themselves truly divine signs and miracles, and could not be said to be displayed ‘toward others’ (εἰς ἄλλους), ‘in others’; but they could well be said εἰς ἀνθρώπους, ‘in men’: for the Saviour God himself is truly man, thus [sancitatus] by the power of divinity, as Paul is witness, and lifted up into heaven. Turrianus waters it down. One who spoke of the raising and healing of others (for ἀνάληψις too, in approved authors and grammarians, is healing, and so is ἀνάρρωσις) would indeed commit no fault by keeping εἰς ἄλλους, which had pleased me too at first; but that is rather harsh, and remoter from the simplicity of Maximus’s ecclesiastical style, in which he gladly uses the sacred and received words themselves; otherwise it is very easy for the abbreviated τὸ ἀνοῦς, that is ἀνθρώπους, to be changed into ἄλλους [the note ends here in print, with no final stop].

text: (b) Ἐξουσιαστικὸς ὑπάρχων, καὶ τῆς τῶν ἁπάντων ἐξουσίας δημιουργός. Ex Dei nativa libertate, suique juris potestate, et quod ejusdem in naturis intelligentibus potestatis auctor ipse sit, recte suadet Maximus, non factum fuisse ἄνουν ἄνθρωπον, hominem mente destitutum; quæ ejus liberæ suique juris potestatis, principium est. Non bene itaque Turr. habens potestatem secundum naturam, et auctor substantiæ omnium; nempe pro ἐξουσίας, legens οὐσίας: quod nec sic ita ejus habuit cod., sic fuit dec[…]dum, ἐξουσιαστής, inter nomina Christi habetur Isa. ix, 6, quod tamen cum aliis a LXX positis, sanctus Hieronymus non exponit. Ejus loco reliqui interpret. δυνατὸς habent. Sonat maxime in potestatem illam, qua quis vel sibi ipse, vel aliis dominatur ac præcipit. Sic ἐξουσιαστικὰ verba appellantur, ἄρχω, κυριεύω, βασιλεύω, et quæ sunt ejus generis. Hinc τὸ αὐτεξούσιον, quod nostri vocant Liberum arbitrium, facultatem scilicet rationis sui dominæ, ac se moventis ex præconcepto fine.
anchorLine: τῆς τῶν ἁπάντων ἐξουσίας δημιουργὸς (b), οὐκ ἄνους γέγονεν ἄνθρωπος
en: ‘Having authority (ἐξουσιαστικός), and maker of the authority of all things.’ From God’s native freedom and his power over his own right, and from the fact that he himself is the author of that same power in intelligent natures, Maximus rightly argues that there was not made an ἄνους ἄνθρωπος, a man bereft of mind; for this is the principle of his free power over his own right. Turrianus therefore does not do well [to render] ‘having power according to nature, and author of the substance of all things’; that is, reading οὐσίας in place of ἐξουσίας; which his codex did not have in that form, so it had to be [dec…dum — word broken in print; probably ‘toned down’]: ἐξουσιαστής is counted among the names of Christ at Isa. 9:6, which however, with the other words set down by the LXX, St Jerome does not explain. In its place the other interpreters have δυνατός. It sounds especially of that power by which a person rules and commands either himself or others. So the verbs ἄρχω, κυριεύω, βασιλεύω and those of that kind are called ἐξουσιαστικά. Hence τὸ αὐτεξούσιον, which our writers call free will, [that is] the faculty of reason as its own mistress, moving itself from a preconceived end.

text: (c) Τῆς πρὸς Μαρῖνον. Non videtur supposita hæc epistola ad Marinum, aliqua esse ex illis quæ ad eum exstant, omnes dogmaticæ: ipsaque prima inter editos Turriano tractatus, serio γνωμικὴν in Christo impugnat voluntatem, et electionem nobis similem, solum admittens quatenus est motus liber, non tamen secundum contraria, aut conjunctam incerti rationem habens; sicque se admisisse Quæst. ad Thalass. excusat ac profitetur. Ubi quoque voluntatem κατ᾽ οἰκείωσιν, per arrogantiam et appropriationem ex Patrum sensu, ipsam nostram voluntatem, quam velut caput membrorum, suam quodammodo ducit, recte exponit; cui nihil commune cum tertia illa Monothelitarum voluntate ut totius, etsi eam etiam illi dicerent κατ᾽ οἰκείωσιν. Quæ seorsum exstat a reliquis Maximi epistolis ejus ad Marinum epistola, qua satisfacit pro adjecta particula Filioque Litteris apostolicis, num ejusmodi aliquid habuerit incertum est, cum nec illi qui Maximo abrogant, ejus quidquam insimulaverint. vel exemplum illius magis integrum, quam modo habeamus, nacti sint. Potuit sic ab iis Græcis ablegari, qui Phòtiani dogmatis studiosiores, Maximi piam illam expositionem ejusque εἰρηνικὸν non probaverunt.
anchorLine: πρὸς Μαρῖνον (c), ὡς φασι, γεγονυίας ἡμῖν τὸν πρεσβύτερον
en: On ‘the one to Marinus’ (Τῆς πρὸς Μαρῖνον). This letter to Marinus does not seem to be spurious, [but] to be some one of those which survive addressed to him, all of them dogmatic; and the first of them, among those printed by Turrianus, seriously opposes a gnomic will (γνωμικήν) in Christ, and an election like ours, admitting it only so far as it is a free motion, yet not one according to contraries, nor having the conjoined notion of uncertainty; and so he excuses and professes that he admitted it in the Questions to Thalassius. Where also he rightly explains the will ‘by appropriation’ (κατ᾽ οἰκείωσιν), by arrogation and appropriation in the sense of the Fathers, [as] our own will, which he in a manner counts his own, as the head of the members; with which that third will of the Monothelites, [a will] of the whole, has nothing in common, even if they too called it κατ᾽ οἰκείωσιν. As to the letter to Marinus that stands apart from Maximus’s other letters, in which he gives satisfaction about the particle Filioque added to the apostolic letters, whether it contained anything of that kind is uncertain, since not even those who deny it to Maximus have charged him with anything. Or [they] may have obtained a copy of it more complete than the one we now have. It could thus have been got rid of by those Greeks who, more zealous for the Photian teaching, did not approve Maximus’s pious exposition and his peaceable statement (εἰρηνικόν).

text:
Maximi locum ex epistola ad Marinum, de processione Spiritus ex Patre et Filio in Martini primi synodicis, quo offensi sint Constantinopolitani, ipseque Maximus exposuerit, ut non duas causas, sed unam, Patrem, Latini sentiant; nonnulli, etiam Catholici, an sit Maximi addubitant; vereorque ne Leo Allatius liberalior sit, in Vindiciis synodi Ephesinæ Cyrilli ea de re, cap. 72, cum ait plerosque addubitare. Anastasius in Collectaneis ut certæ fidei retulit, ac momentum habere in rem fidei et Ecclesiæ existimavit. In concilio Lugdunensi Gregorio X pontifice, nescio qui dubitarint: non Beccus, non Georgius Metochita, etc. In Florentino ea Maximi distinctione et sententia, Ecclesiarum pax conciliata: non Blemidas aliique Catholici ex schismaticis, Palamas, Marcus Ephesius, etc. Libri antiquissimi servarunt, in quibus codex ille Romanus antiquior vii synodo, ex quo exscriptus Reg. Michaele Duca Angelo Comneno imper. Qui dubitent, parum versatos in Maximi lectione existimo, nec ullam arbitror exstare ejus epistolam aut tomum dogmaticum, in quo ejus styli character clarius eluceat, quibus præsertim præfatur, ut in aliis ad eumdem Marinum dogmaticis, aliosque viros sacros, diversi argumenti epistolis. Nec sic a vero et catholico sensu abhorret Maximi expressio, ut tam facile ejus relinquendum vadimonium viro catholico sit. Una causa Pater absolute, seu auctor: nec Filius auctor, nisi quia a Patre, et ejus quasi virtus, quo cum una causa, et principium de principio: quod Græci libentius particula per exprimunt, ut ordinem significent, et Patri τὸ προκαταρκτικόν, ratione primæ causæ et originalis (a se scilicet) servent. Operæ pretium igitur fecit Maximus, qui et vivus, et vita functus, dissentaneas in specie Doctorum voces Virorumque Ecclesiasticorum eodem sensu, velut olim Athanasius in eadem prope materia (ac περὶ Θεολογίας) commiserit.
Locum Maximi eo ipso sensu egregie exponit Joan. Veccus, orat. 2, t. II Græciæ orth. p. 63 et 64, ubi omissa fusiori explicatione, quam Damasceno malit impendere, cujus causa difficilior, et quo adversarii magis glorientur, sic paucis de Maximo: Ὑμῖν δὲ οὐκ ἀγαπητὸν τῷ μεγάλῳ Μαξίμῳ κατακολουθεῖν ὑπερηγορούντι Ῥωμαίων, ἐφ᾽ οἷς καὶ τότε ἐκ Πατρὸς καὶ Υἱοῦ τὸ Πνεῦμα ἔλεγον ἐκπορεύεσθαι· καὶ οὐδὲν διαφέρειν, τὸ ἐκ Πατρὸς δι᾽ Υἱοῦ πρὸς τὸ, ἐξ ἀμφοῖν ἐκδιδάσκοντι· δι᾽ ὧν ἡ ἐπιστολὴ τὸ, ἐκ τοῦ Υἱοῦ ἐκπορεύεσθαι, εἰς τὸ, δι᾽ Υἱοῦ προϊέναι σαφῶς ἐκλαμβάνεται; Ubi Leo All. An non volupe vobis fuerit, magnum Maximum sequi, patrocinium Romanorum suscipientem, qui tum ex Patre et Filio Spiritum procedere affirmabant: nihilque differre ex Patre per Filium, et ex utroque, edocentem: quibus in illa epistola, Ex Filio procedere, in illud, Per Filium procedere, assumitur. Omissa Allatio particula καὶ, ipsa non inutilis, qua significatur esse hoc argumento antiquæ traditioni, cum nulla Ecclesiarum scissione sic Romana Ecclesia doceret, nec Græcam lateret. Vexatque egregie hoc argumentum Georgius Metochita in suis de processione Spiritus sancti quinque libris, a me ipsi Leoni Allatio transmissis, ut in tertium suæ Græciæ orthodoxæ volumen conferret; sicque transmissi tum mihi periere, tum rei ecclesiasticæ. Extrema verba 74 sic redderem: Ea ratione quod epistola, ex Filio procedere, palam exponat, ut sit idem ac per Filium prodire. Fuse vero idem ad Constantinum, l. iv, p. 203 et seq., ubi optime quasi utrique parti de processione Spiritus sancti studentem sanctum Maximum, molliendo illa verba junxisse, ut ad assensum traheret, rixamque sedaret: Ἐξ ὧν οὐκ αἰτίαν τοῦ Πνεύματος τὸν Υἱὸν ποιοῦντας σφᾶς ἑαυτοὺς ἀπέδειξαν. Ostenderunt se non causam Spiritus Filium facere: qualem illi sibi videbantur ex ipsorum verbis et modo profitendi, habere: primam scilicet, et qualis est Pater: quod ipsum illis ex contentione provenerat, et quod Latini Monothelitarum hæresis causa ipsos perstringerent; ut optime idem Veccus, p. 47, dicens se deprehendisse ex Maximi epistola; ac facile quisque advertat: nec aliter in Photio et Cerulario, sic privata odia vertentibus in causam fidei.
In excerpto, ex epistola quam Regius Cod. laudatus Romæ scriptam dicit, Romanus alter, qui solus habet, cum epistola ad Marinum conjungit, quasi sit illius pars: καὶ μεθ᾽ ἕτερα· quomodo non Romæ,
en: [On] the passage of Maximus from the letter to Marinus, about the procession of the Spirit from the Father and the Son, in the synodical letters of Martin I, by which the Constantinopolitans were offended, and which Maximus himself explained so that the Latins hold not two causes but one, the Father: some, even Catholics, doubt whether it is Maximus’s; and I fear that Leo Allatius is rather too liberal, in his Vindication of the Synod of Ephesus of Cyril [Vindiciis synodi Ephesinæ Cyrilli], ch. 72, when he says that most doubt it [plerosque addubitare]. Anastasius in his Collectanea reported it as a matter of certain faith, and judged that it has weight for the faith and the Church. At the Council of Lyons under Pope Gregory X, I do not know who doubted it: not Beccus, not George Metochites, etc. At Florence, by that distinction and judgment of Maximus the peace of the Churches was made: not Blemmydes and other Catholics from the schismatics, [nor] Palamas, Mark of Ephesus, etc. [as printed: ‘non Blemidas aliique Catholici ex schismaticis, Palamas, Marcus Ephesius’]. The most ancient books preserved it, among them that Roman codex older than the Seventh Synod, from which the Regius [codex] was copied under the emperor Michael Doukas Angelos Komnenos. Those who doubt, I judge to be little versed in the reading of Maximus, and I think there exists no letter or dogmatic tome of his in which the character of his style shines out more clearly, especially in those [passages] where he prefaces, as in the other dogmatic letters to the same Marinus, and in letters of different content to other holy men. Nor does Maximus’s expression so far depart from the true and Catholic sense that a Catholic should so easily abandon the pledge [to it]. One cause: the Father absolutely, or author; the Son is not author except in that he is from the Father, and as his power, with which he is one cause, and a principle from a principle; which the Greeks more willingly express by the particle ‘through’, to signify order, and to preserve for the Father the προκαταρκτικόν (‘originating’), by reason of first and original cause (that is, from himself). Maximus therefore did well, who, alive and having ended his life, brought together in one sense voices that in appearance disagree, of Doctors and of Ecclesiastical men, as Athanasius did once on nearly the same subject (also on theology). John Veccus, Oration 2, vol. II of his Græcia orthodoxa, pp. 63 and 64, explains Maximus’s passage splendidly in that very sense, where, omitting a fuller explanation, which he prefers to give to Damascene, whose case is harder and over which the adversaries boast more, he says briefly of Maximus: [Greek, quoted:] ‘It is not agreeable to you to follow the great Maximus, who speaks up for the Romans, on account of which they then said that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; and that there is no difference between “from the Father through the Son” and “from both”, teaching; by which the letter’s “to proceed from the Son” is clearly taken as “to go forth through the Son”?’ [my rendering of the Greek, which is partly broken in print]. Here Leo Allatius [says]: ‘Would it not please you to follow the great Maximus, who undertakes the defence of the Romans, who then affirmed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son: and teaches that there is no difference between from the Father through the Son and from both: in which letter “to proceed from the Son” is taken up into “to proceed through the Son”.’ Allatius omits the particle καί, itself not useless, by which it is shown that this is an argument from ancient tradition, since the Roman Church taught so with no division of the Churches, and it was not hidden from the Greek [Church]. George Metochites vigorously presses this argument in his five books on the procession of the Holy Spirit, which I sent to Leo Allatius himself, to bring into the third volume of his Græcia orthodoxa; and so they, when sent, were lost, both to me and to the ecclesiastical cause. The last words I would render thus: ‘In the sense that the letter says [the Spirit] proceeds from the Son, it plainly explains it so that it is the same as to go forth through the Son.’ At length, too, [Veccus] to Constantine, book 4, p. 203 ff., where [he shows] very well that holy Maximus, as one concerned for both parties on the procession of the Holy Spirit, joined those words by softening them, in order to draw them to assent and calm the quarrel: [Greek:] ‘from which they showed themselves not to be making the Son the cause of the Spirit.’ They showed that they were not making the Son a cause of the Spirit: such as they seemed to themselves, from their own words and manner of speaking, to hold: a first [cause], that is, and such as the Father is; which had arisen for them from the dispute, and because the Latins accused them [the Greeks] of the heresy of the Monothelites; as the same Veccus says very well, p. 47, saying that he gathered this from Maximus’s letter; and anyone may readily notice that it was no otherwise in Photius and Cerularius, who turned private hatreds into a cause of the faith. In the excerpt from the letter which the Regius codex, cited above, says was written at Rome — the other, Roman [codex], which alone has it, joins it to the letter to Marinus, as if it were a part of it: καὶ μεθ᾽ ἕτερα (‘and after other things’) — how not at Rome,

text:
sed Byzacii in Africa scripta esset. Ac num imperitus librarius Byzantium sibi pro Byzacio divinavit, ut eamdem epistolam, eodem loco scriptam sibi finxerit? Anastasius, quod non defloravit, nec habuit: nunquam omissurus sic illustre Romanæ fidei et Ecclesiæ, Petri privilegio, testimonium ac elogium. Nihil autem abhorret a Maximi aliis, quibus per occasionem Romanos laudat, eorumque in fide firmitatem: nusquam non fidei primatum et arcem Ecclesiasticæ communionis, in Romano Antistite ponens, a quo et absolutio ab hæresi impetranda sit, ac cujus arbitratu transigenda fidei negotia.
Movere possit, quod sex synodos numerat, cum sexta synodus Maximo jam consummato celebrata sit. Existimo sextam voluisse ipsam Romanam et Lateranensem Martino I pontifice, quæ pro sui celebritate sic quinque generalibus Maximo comnumerari potuit: qua vere Catholicis supremo judicio confossa hydra videretur, cui interfuisset aut communicasset, quidquid esset orthodoxum, reliquis per Orientem sedibus, excepta Hierosolymitana, Monothelitarum hæresi infectis: in qua perinde Sophronio auctore ea damnata fuerat, uti etiam a Joan. IV Romæ: sed non ea pompa et celebritate, qua a Martino e concilio Lateranensi, Maximo ipso illi incentore, cujus acta illustrissima exstarent, in quibus ventilata omnia, adductaque Scripturæ ac Patrum testimonia, quibus veritas catholica lucidissime statueretur, ac quidquid Monothelitarum furfuris esset, exsufflaretur, illorum etiam nominatim proscriptis capitibus: ut jam una Christianitatis tessera viderentur, in sancta una catholica, quo tantum sui desiderium per Orientem veris fidelibus consciverant, quantum Theodosius Gangrensis presbyter testatur in Hypomnestico. Nec ultra trahenda Maximi epistola ad Petrum illustrem, quam nobis servarit Anastasius in Collectaneis excerptam, unaque nobis Græce desideratur: cum alia dogmatica nobis exstent ad eumdem, in epistolis, quas sequentibus repræsento.
en: […how not at Rome,] but written at Byzacium in Africa? And did an unskilled copyist, guessing Byzantium for Byzacium, invent for himself the same letter written in the same place? Anastasius, [for the part] he did not cull, he also did not have: he would never have omitted so illustrious a testimony and praise of the Roman faith and Church, of Peter’s privilege. Nor is it at all at odds with Maximus’s other letters, in which on occasion he praises the Romans and their firmness in the faith: everywhere placing the primacy of faith and the citadel of ecclesiastical communion in the Roman Bishop, from whom absolution from heresy is to be obtained and at whose judgment the business of the faith is to be settled. It might raise a difficulty that he counts six synods, when the sixth synod was held after Maximus had finished his course. I think he meant the Roman synod itself, the Lateran under Pope Martin I, which, for its renown, could be reckoned by Maximus with the five general councils: in which the hydra of the Monothelites was truly pierced by the supreme judgment of Catholics, [and] whoever had taken part or communicated, whatever was orthodox, while the other sees of the East, Jerusalem excepted, were infected with the Monothelite heresy: in which [the heresy] had been condemned likewise at the instigation of Sophronius, as also by John IV at Rome: but not with that pomp and renown with which it was condemned by Martin in the Lateran council, Maximus himself being its instigator, whose most illustrious acts survive, in which everything was debated, and testimonies of Scripture and the Fathers adduced, by which Catholic truth would be most clearly established, and whatever of the Monothelite chaff there was would be blown away, their leaders being proscribed by name, so that they might now appear a single badge of Christianity, in the one holy catholic [Church], for which true believers throughout the East had conceived as great a longing as Theodosius, priest of Gangra, bears witness in his Hypomnesticum. Nor is Maximus’s letter to Peter the Illustrious to be stretched further, which Anastasius preserved for us, excerpted, in his Collectanea, and which alone is lacking to us in Greek: since other dogmatic letters of his to the same man survive, among the letters which I reproduce in what follows.

text: (d) Ex Regio cod. collato cum nostro Tiliano S. Hilarii et Dufresnii editisque Latine a Turriano. Eadem fere Leontius. Opusculum hoc ipsum breve, quod tam multis codd. exstat, argumento est, pluris Ecclesiæ catholicæ alumnis olim habitum, eisque velut tesseræ loco fuisse adversus hæreticos, qui vel de Deitate male sensissent, vel de dispensatione seu incarnatione; ne omissa quidem Macedonii hæresi, in nostro sancti Hilarii cod., sive ipse sanctus Maximus illam inseruit, sive alius quispiam studiosus adjecit, ut esset plenior doctrina; quod vero similius putem, vel inde quod in aliis ubique codd. desideratur. Placuit vero etiam repræsentare. Titulus apud Turr. paulo auctior; addit enim, Et quod Arius et Nestorius in theologia et incarnatione, contra atque Sabellius et Eutyches sentiant: quod ipsum indicat, unum hoc Maximum spectasse, ut contrarias has hæreses in Trinitate et Incarnatione contenderet, eisque fidem catholicam, ipsam illarum mediam, opponeret.
anchorLine: Περὶ τῶν δύο τοῦ Χριστοῦ φύσεων (d).
en: From the Regius codex, collated with our Tilianus of St Hilary [Tiliano S. Hilarii] and with Dufresne’s, and with the Latin editions by Turrianus. Leontius is nearly the same. This very opuscule, short as it is, which survives in so many codices, is proof that it was once highly esteemed by many sons of the Catholic Church and served them as a sort of watchword against heretics who thought wrongly either about the Godhead or about the dispensation, that is the incarnation; nor is the heresy of Macedonius omitted, in our codex of St Hilary, whether Maximus himself inserted it or some zealous person added it to make the teaching fuller; I think the latter more likely, also because it is lacking everywhere in the other codices. I decided to reproduce it as well. The title in Turrianus is somewhat longer, for he adds ‘and that Arius and Nestorius think, in theology and in the incarnation, contrary to Sabellius and Eutyches’; which itself shows that Maximus had this one aim, to set these opposing heresies in the Trinity and the Incarnation against each other and to oppose to them the Catholic faith, which stands midway between them.

text: (e) Καὶ Θεὸν πῶς διαβεβαιοῖ. Sic noster ille cod. non enclitice. Qui velit τὸ, πῶς, ἐμφατικῶς dici, ac velut quadam admiratione, nihil ipse inficias ierim. Sic certe quod altero statim numero sequitur, Πῶς ἡ ἄκρα ἕνωσις, admiratione reddo; quidquid Turrianus interrogatione: Quomodo summa unio et idem habet et diversum? Non id quærit Maximus, sed admiratur, in divinis æque ac in creatis: nisi quod in divinis, non satis aptum, τὸ, diversum et diversitas, quod sic proclive Turr. usurpat: pro eo quod est distinctum et distinctio, sed aliud, vel alterum, vel differens ac differentia; quod nimirum diversus divisionem videatur inducere; sicque reddit Ambros. Calep. diversus, separatus, κεχωρισμένος: quo facit illud Cæsaris De bello Afr.: Cum Numidas diversos dissipatosque in omnes partes fugere vidissent; itemque Plauti in Rud.: Inde suam quisque ibant diversi domum. Ἑτερότητα dicant, si liceret, castigatiores theologi, alietatem; uti etiam alia eis persona atque alia in divinis dicitur: quanquam ἕτερος respectu duorum proprie, ἄλλος etiam plurium. Ad illa verba Hilariani nostri cod. ἢ ταυτότητα οὐσιῶν, addo quæ necessaria sunt, ut sit plenus sensus, καὶ ἑτερότητα προσώπων, καὶ τὸ ἔμπαλιν. Aliter enim se res in Deo habet, aliter in Christo ac nobis, modoque opposito; quod utrumque propositum exponere Maximo, cum utrobique summa unio sit, altera essentialis seu natura, altera personalis ac subsistentia.
anchorLine: Θεὸν πῶς διαβεβαιοῖ (e). Ὁμοίως καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς
en: ‘And how he affirms God.’ So our codex, not enclitically. Whoever wants τὸ πῶς (‘how’) said emphatically, and as with a certain wonder, I would not deny. So certainly I render with wonder what follows at once in the next number, ‘How the highest union has both sameness and otherness’ (Πῶς ἡ ἄκρα ἕνωσις); whereas Turrianus [renders it] by a question, ‘How does the highest union have both the same and the diverse?’ Maximus is not asking this but wondering, in divine things as in created; except that in divine matters the words ‘diversum’ and ‘diversitas’ are not quite apt, which Turrianus readily uses for ‘distinctum’ and ‘distinctio’, but [they mean] ‘other’, or ‘another’, or ‘differing’ and ‘difference’; since ‘diversus’ seems to bring in division; and so Ambrosius Calepinus renders ‘diversus’ as ‘separate’ (κεχωρισμένος): to which belongs Caesar’s phrase in the African War, ‘when they saw the Numidians scattered and fleeing in every direction’, and likewise Plautus in the Rudens, ‘thence each went his way, in different directions, home’. The more careful theologians would say ἑτερότης, if it were allowed, ‘alietas’; as also one person and another is said in divine matters: although ἕτερος properly regards two, ἄλλος more than two. To those words of our Hilarian codex, ἢ ταυτότητα οὐσιῶν, I add what is necessary to complete the sense, ‘and the otherness of persons, and the reverse’. For the matter stands one way in God, another in Christ and in us, and in the opposite manner; each proposition Maximus had to set out, since in both there is the highest union, the one essential or of nature, the other personal and of subsistence.

text: (f) Διὰ τὸ μὴ ἰδιοϋπόστατον. Nec Turrianus aliam habuerit vocem, vel Maximus aliam scripserit. Quod ergo reddit: Et propter propriam sententiam dic unam hypostasim, omissa scilicet particula negante, ejus propositio minime sana sit. Quæ enim theologia, ut propter subsistentiam propriam duplicis substantiæ Verbi et carnis, quam scilicet proprie ac seorsim, propriamque sibi quodque horum vindicet, una in Christo dicenda sit hypostasis aut persona? non econtra, quod non sit propria, sed communis per unitionem facta ut omnes nostri codd. repræsentant: debuitque vir doctus ac pius, vel si ita illi laborabat ejus cod. aberatque negatio, non tam facile decoquere. Sic quoque num. 4 et 5. male illi desiderata negatio, cujus absentia, ipsa statim simplex propositio offendit, etsi in vi hypotheticæ verus sensus utcumque elici queat.
anchorLine: …διὰ τοῦ μὴ ἰδιοϋπόστατον (f), μίαν ὑπόστασιν λέγε.
en: ‘Because it is not a hypostasis of its own [Διὰ τὸ μὴ ἰδιοϋπόστατον].’ Neither would Turrianus have had another word, nor Maximus have written another. What he therefore renders, ‘and by reason of a proper sentiment/subsistence say one hypostasis’ [Et propter propriam sententiam dic unam hypostasim], omitting the negating particle, makes his proposition not at all sound. For what theology would it be, that by reason of the proper subsistence of the twofold substance of the Word and of the flesh, which each of them claims as its own, properly and separately, one hypostasis or person should be said in Christ? On the contrary, [it is said] because it is not proper but common, made through the union, as all our codices represent: and the learned and pious man should, even if his own codex had it so and lacked the negation, not so easily have toned it down. So also at nos. 4 and 5 he wrongly missed the negation, whose absence offends the bare proposition at once, though in the force of a hypothetical a true sense can somehow be drawn out.
